paragraphs: Those who see no evil in the silence of heretics should first consider that heretical opinions never receive a fair and thorough discussion. Those that could not withstand it may be stopped from spreading, but they do not disappear.

Yet it is not the minds of heretics that suffer most from the ban on every inquiry which does not end in orthodox conclusions. The greatest harm falls on those who are not heretics. Their whole mental development is cramped, and their reason cowed, by the fear of heresy. Who can compute what the world loses in the many promising intellects joined to timid characters? Such people dare not follow any bold, independent train of thought, for fear it might lead them to something irreligious or immoral. Among them we sometimes meet a man of deep conscientiousness and refined understanding, who spends his life in subtle reasoning with an intellect he cannot silence. He exhausts his ingenuity in trying to reconcile his conscience and reason with orthodoxy, perhaps never succeeding.

No one can be a great thinker who does not recognise that his first duty as a thinker is to follow his intellect wherever it may lead. Truth gains more from the errors of someone who thinks for himself, with due study, than from the true opinions of those who hold them only because they do not allow themselves to think.

Not that freedom of thought is required solely, or chiefly, to form great thinkers. It is as necessary, and even more so, to enable average human beings to attain the mental stature of which they are capable. There have been, and may again be, great individual thinkers in an atmosphere of mental slavery. But there never has been, nor ever will be, an intellectually active people in that atmosphere. When a people briefly approached such a character, it was because the dread of heterodox speculation had been suspended for a time. Sometimes there is a tacit agreement that principles are not to be disputed and that the greatest questions of humanity are closed. Then we cannot hope for the high level of mental activity which made certain periods of history so remarkable. When controversy avoided subjects large enough to kindle enthusiasm, the mind of a people was never stirred from its foundations. Nor did it receive the impulse that raised even persons of ordinary intellect to something of the dignity of thinking beings.

Europe offers three examples. The first is the period immediately following the Reformation. The second is the speculative movement of the latter half of the eighteenth century, limited to the Continent and to a more cultivated class. The third, briefer still, is the intellectual ferment of Germany in the age of Goethe and Fichte. These periods differed widely in the opinions they developed. They were alike, however, in that the yoke of authority was broken in all three. An old mental despotism had been thrown off, and no new one had yet taken its place. The impulse of these three periods has made Europe what it now is. Every improvement in the human mind or in institutions can be traced to one of them. Lately, all three impulses have seemed almost spent. We can expect no fresh start until we again assert our mental freedom.
